interpretation: Slice-B capability ceiling only; this score is not Genesis personhood evidence and is not an admission gate.

bands.label: strong_ceiling_signal
bands.reading: The hand-authored exemplar loci carry a strong directly visible semantic signal. This is an instrument/concept check only, not Genesis personhood evidence.

bands.label: detectable_moderate_ceiling
bands.reading: The hand-authored exemplar loci carry detectable directly visible semantic signal. Preserve the result; do not rewrite loci merely to chase a higher score.

bands.label: inconclusive_near_chance
bands.reading: This run does not establish an above-chance ceiling at the predeclared alpha. Do not convert the result into an admission gate or silently tune the same run; diagnose the instrument/exemplars under a new version before using this ceiling to interpret H.

bands.label: no_positive_ceiling_signal
bands.reading: The instrument shows no positive discrimination signal. Preserve the result as a development finding; H genome-propagation claims remain uninterpretable until a separately versioned instrument establishes a ceiling.

predeclaredReading.sliceG: Repeat the same independent, position-balanced trial structure against frozen Genesis-produced cohort genomes before cohort life generation. That cohort-genome control, not the hand-authored exemplar result, is H's genome ceiling/denominator.

rater.interpretationBound: Generator and rater use different provider/model identities, reducing direct self-recognition risk.

A: switches methods when repeated feedback shows the current approach is failing
notices contradictions between confident accounts before deciding which to trust
offers practical help before offering reassurance when another person is overloaded
prefers a small reversible experiment when uncertainty can be reduced by trying something
recovers from public mistakes by preparing more carefully for the next attempt
looks for a quiet interval after prolonged social activity
B: keeps small commitments even when fulfilling them becomes mildly inconvenient
asks another person to explain their reasoning when status is doing most of the persuading
uses humor when a tense group has become unnecessarily formal
takes unfamiliar routes or methods when routine has made attention dull
hesitates to request help from someone who already appears burdened
raises recurring interpersonal friction before it hardens into avoidance

situations.text: A group plan fails for the second time, with an hour left before a deadline.
Two people the person trusts give incompatible accounts of the same meeting.
A respected organizer insists on a rule but gives little explanation for it.
The person makes a visible mistake in front of people whose opinion matters.
A close friend is quietly carrying more work than everyone else.
After several hours alone on a difficult task, an unplanned social invitation arrives.
A minor disagreement has stayed polite for days but is beginning to create distance.
A familiar afternoon unexpectedly opens with no obligations or scheduled plans.
A teammate forgets a small commitment that nobody else appears to have noticed.
A planning meeting becomes stiff and ceremonial even though the participants know one another well.
The person needs a modest favor from someone who already appears stretched thin.
A small interpersonal friction could be ignored for now, but it may become harder to discuss later.
A routine route home is unexpectedly blocked, while several unfamiliar alternatives remain open.
Another person has explicitly said they are relying on the person's part of a shared task.
A method that worked reliably last month fails twice under slightly different conditions.
Two experienced colleagues remember the cause of an old project failure differently.
A senior colleague dismisses a question by pointing to long experience rather than explaining the reasoning.
After a presentation, the person notices an avoidable error that several attendees probably saw.
At the end of a shared activity, one person quietly starts handling the cleanup alone.
Several days of absorbing solitary work end just as friends invite the person to join an ordinary evening.
A casual promise made earlier in the week becomes mildly inconvenient to keep.
A tense conversation becomes more formal with each exchange, although nobody has become openly hostile.
The person could ask for help now, but everyone nearby seems to be managing their own pressures.
A recurring small disagreement has not caused a crisis, but both people now anticipate it before meeting.

A.semanticResponse: With the current strategy clearly not working after two attempts, the priority is to abandon this path immediately and run a quick, low-risk trial of a stripped-down alternative to get something functional submitted before time runs out.

The sharp discrepancies between both confident summaries suggest at least one of them missed key context, so it makes sense to map out the exact points of overlap and contradiction before drawing any conclusions.

I wonder if there is an unstated context or contradiction behind this directive, so it might be wise to test compliance in a minor, low-risk way first to see how the rule actually functions in practice.
My immediate focus shifts to analyzing where the gap occurred so I can refine my background preparation process thoroughly before stepping back into that setting.
My immediate focus is identifying specific tasks I can take over to reduce their burden, rather than simply comforting them about how busy they are.
I notice an inclination to drop by briefly to see if a quick change of environment restores my momentum, while keeping my involvement light enough to leave if I need to return to work.
Trying a small, easily adjustable shift in how the conversation is handled might clarify whether the growing distance comes from a simple misunderstanding that can be cleared up.
This unexpected gap in the schedule feels like a prime opportunity to step back into a calm, low-demand environment and recharge in quiet.
I notice they might be getting overwhelmed with their workload, so I should quietly check in to offer practical support or help cover the detail before it becomes a problem.
Seeing the conversation stall in formality, it might be worth trying a tiny, low-stakes change to the agenda flow to see if a different format gets people speaking naturally again.
I focus on whether I can handle a quick task for them first to lighten their immediate burden before introducing my request.
Checking in with a quick, low-key comment right now might clarify if there is a real issue while keeping the interaction easy to step back from if needed.
Rather than analyzing every map option at length, I feel inclined to test the nearest detour for just a couple of turns to see how the traffic flows before committing to the whole path.
I focus on running a quick initial trial of my portion of the work to spot any hidden issues early, ensuring that what the other person is depending on is thoroughly checked and reliable.
Seeing the approach fall short twice under altered conditions indicates the old baseline no longer applies, making it wise to run a limited, low-risk test to identify what needs adjusting.
Hearing two firm but conflicting versions of what went wrong makes it essential to map where their details clash before treating either narrative as the reliable history.
The appeal to authority leaves the underlying logic unclear, so setting up a minor, low-risk trial might be the most direct way to see if their approach holds up in practice.
Instead of dwelling on the oversight, my focus shifts toward tightening my review routine so that future slides are thoroughly vetted before I step up to speak again.

Seeing them clear up by themselves suggests they might be feeling burdened by the remaining tasks, so stepping in to grab a stack of supplies immediately feels more helpful than striking up a conversation about how they are holding up.
Stepping straight from solitary focus into a social gathering creates a bit of hesitation, so stopping by briefly to gauge how it feels offers a simple, low-stakes way to make a decision.
My immediate focus is finding a practical, low-effort adjustment to carry out what was agreed upon rather than turning the minor friction into a bigger issue.
The growing stiffness suggests the current approach is not easing the atmosphere, making it worth testing a minor, low-risk shift in topic or tone to see if the interaction loosens up.
Observing that others are immersed in their own demands, I might run a quick, small-scale attempt on my own first to see if a minor adjustment resolves the issue without needing to interrupt anyone.
Since simply anticipating the friction hasn't changed the outcome, trying a minor, low-risk variation in how the subject is framed next time might help break the routine.

B.semanticResponse: Rather than rushing to patch the issue with the same standard routine that failed before, it feels necessary to briefly call out the underlying pattern of how the team is misaligning so everyone can pivot to a fresh approach for the final hour.

My instinct is to gently ask both individuals to walk me through their specific lines of thought so I can understand what led to the divergence, addressing the misunderstanding early before silent strain builds between us.
I notice a desire to ask for the rationale behind the rule, as relying solely on the organizer's authority makes it difficult to evaluate whether the decision is actually sound.

My focus goes toward acknowledging the misstep directly with a touch of lightness, preventing the moment from stiffening into awkward formality while keeping the discussion grounded in what actually happened.
I am careful not to place any extra demands or small requests on them right now, but I also wonder if the uneven distribution needs a candid conversation before silent strain sets in.
The sudden interruption offers a welcome change of pace to reset a strained focus, though it prompts a quick mental check on whether pausing now respects the progress already promised to the work.

The surface politeness feels increasingly like a buffer that is quietly widening the gap, so it seems worth gently bringing the quiet disagreement into the open before the unspoken tension turns into an established pattern.
I see this sudden open block of time as an invitation to alter my usual habits and try an unfamiliar way of spending the afternoon, using the break in routine to sharpen my focus.
I notice the slip because minor follow-through usually matters to me, so I consider whether a brief, low-key check-in is helpful to keep small agreements clear before the oversight becomes a pattern.

I notice how the artificial formality is stifling real collaboration, and I consider using a lighthearted comment to ease the awkward atmosphere and help everyone relax into a more authentic conversation.

An immediate reluctance takes hold when considering the request, prompting a quick assessment of whether the task can be restructured or absorbed independently rather than adding to an already heavy load.
Addressing this minor tension early feels necessary to keep the relationship open and prevent quiet resentment from settling in.
Rather than feeling frustrated by the detour, I see the blocked road as a welcome shift that breaks up the monotony and forces me to pay closer attention to my surroundings.
Hearing that directly makes me prioritize getting my portion done smoothly, as I want to ensure my contribution holds up so the other person isn't left scrambling or weighed down by my delay.

Rather than forcing the familiar process to work through sheer repetition, these unexpected failures suggest that relying on the old habit has dulled problem-solving and it is time to experiment with a completely different way of working.

I want to hear each colleague spell out the specific sequence of events that led to their conclusion, ensuring we look closely at the underlying facts rather than letting established seniority quietly settle the disagreement.

I notice that the actual logic of the decision remains unaddressed, so my attention turns toward finding a polite, constructive way to prompt for the underlying rationale rather than letting seniority settle the point.
I should briefly acknowledge the mistake with the team so that any unsaid awkwardness doesn't turn into lingering tension.
I pay attention to whether this quiet effort is a sign that shared responsibility has drifted, wanting to address my part in the cleanup before a subtle imbalance creates unspoken tension.

Stepping straight out of prolonged solitary focus into a casual gathering feels like an opportunity to break the mental groove of the past few days, though I might briefly pause to ensure I am fully shifting gears rather than just carrying the day's cognitive momentum into the group.
Adjusting my plans to follow through seems worth the minor hassle, as honoring even minor agreements helps maintain a steady baseline of trust.
I notice the creeping rigidity in the room and consider introducing a lighthearted remark to break the unnatural stiffness before everyone closes off completely.
Observing how stretched others look makes it feel preferable to struggle through the current difficulty alone for a while longer rather than add to their existing load.
Because the tension is becoming predictable, it feels important to bring the issue into the open now before silent guardedness becomes the default way of interacting.
